opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I've genuinely gone back and forth on, and I think the honest answer is that there are real advantages on both sides.

At a grantmaking organization like Open Phil, the main thing you have is leverage and breadth. You're not just doing one research agenda; you're looking across the whole landscape of people working on AI safety and AI forecasting and trying to figure out where the marginal dollar or the marginal bit of attention does the most good. That bird's-eye view is valuable. You see a lot of different bets, you can notice gaps, and you can help seed entire organizations or research directions that wouldn't otherwise exist. Frankly, places like Redwood and METR are partly the kind of thing that funding ecosystem exists to make possible.

The downside is that you're one step removed from the object level. You're often evaluating other people's work rather than getting your hands dirty, and I think there's a real risk that your models of what's going on get a little stale or abstract. When the field is moving as fast as it is now, there's a lot of value in being close to the actual systems: running evals, seeing where models surprise you, having opinions that come from direct contact with the empirical reality rather than from reading other people's write-ups.

An organization like METR is interesting to me precisely because it sits at the intersection of things I care about. A lot of my older work was about forecasting: when will we get transformative AI, how should we think about the trajectory? METR is trying to answer a very empirical version of that question: what can these models actually do right now, how fast is that improving, and how close are we to dangerous capability thresholds? That's a really direct way to make the forecasting conversation less speculative. Redwood is more focused on control and on what concrete safety techniques look like if you take seriously the possibility that models might be working against you. That's also extremely important, and in some ways it's the more "build the thing" end of the spectrum.

So the way I frame the tradeoff for myself is roughly: comparative advantage, plus what the field needs most at this particular moment. A few years ago, I think the bottleneck was more conceptual. People didn't have shared frameworks for thinking about timelines or about what could go wrong, and writing big reports and doing grantmaking was a decent way to contribute. Today I think the bottleneck has shifted toward high-quality empirical evidence that decision-makers, labs and governments in particular, will actually take seriously. If that's right, there's a strong case for being closer to where that evidence is produced.

But I don't think there's a universally correct answer. Some people are much more valuable as funders and strategists than as researchers, and moving them to the bench would be a loss. The question I try to ask is: if I'm not doing this, who is, and how much worse would it be? Sometimes the answer points toward staying put, and sometimes it points toward going where the action is.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Open Phil’s broad, landscape-wide grantmaking role with closer, more hands-on work on narrower missions at METR or Redwood.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, actually. The honest answer is that there's a real tension, and I don't think I've fully resolved it.

The case for going to a place like Redwood or METR is pretty straightforward. Those are organizations doing object-level work, where the feedback loops are tighter. You run an experiment, you get a result, you learn something. At OpenPhil, a lot of what I do is thinking about where money should go, writing up worldviews, trying to forecast what the field will look like in five years. And that work matters, but it's much harder to tell when you're wrong. You can write a report and the world sort of nods and moves on, and you don't get the kind of sharp signal that tells you your model was off.

The case for staying is that grantmaking has leverage that's genuinely hard to replicate. If I'm at a research org, I'm one researcher, or one manager of a team. At OpenPhil, the decisions about which orgs exist at all, which approaches get funded enough to find out whether they work, those flow through a fairly small number of people. And I think the field is still at a stage where those allocation decisions are really consequential. There aren't that many people who have both the technical context and the willingness to sit with the big-picture questions long enough to make good calls.

There's also a comparative advantage thing. I've spent years building up a particular kind of judgment about timelines and threat models and which research directions seem promising. That's not nothing, and it's more useful in a funder seat than it would be as, say, the person writing the eval harness.

But I'll admit the pull toward object-level work is partly emotional. It's more satisfying to be close to the thing. And I do worry that staying too far from the frontier for too long makes your grantmaking judgment worse, because you start reasoning from a model of the field that's a couple years stale. So I try to counteract that by staying really engaged with what the grantees are actually finding, rather than just reading the summaries.

If I had to put it in one line: I think the marginal grantmaker with good technical taste is scarcer right now than the marginal technical researcher, so I've stayed. But I hold that pretty loosely, and I could see it flipping.

astra-6.text:
I think the central question for me is where my marginal contribution is greatest. At Open Phil, I can help decide which projects get funded, identify gaps in the ecosystem, and help people get new things off the ground. That can be a lot of leverage, especially if the alternative is that a promising project simply doesn’t happen.

But there’s also a real appeal to being inside an organization like Redwood or METR, where you’re much closer to the actual research. You get faster feedback, you build a more concrete understanding of what’s hard, and you can take responsibility for making a particular thing work. As a funder, it’s easier to have a view that sounds reasonable but hasn’t really been tested against those details.

So I’d want to compare specific roles, rather than funding versus research in the abstract. Is there a particular bottleneck at one of those organizations that I’m unusually well suited to address? And how much of what I’m doing at Open Phil could someone else pick up? Those counterfactuals matter more to me than which job seems more directly connected to the problem.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Open Phil’s broad funding and ecosystem work with being closer to research, gaining deeper feedback, and taking responsibility for a specific project or bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main tradeoff is between getting a really tight feedback loop on one particular problem and having a broader view of where resources could be most useful. At a place like Redwood or METR, you’re building things, running experiments, and finding out where your picture was wrong. There’s a lot of value in that kind of direct contact with the work.

At Open Phil, you’re a step removed, which has real costs. But you can also ask, “What’s missing from the ecosystem? Which teams should exist that don’t exist yet? Where could additional funding make a big difference?” And if you have useful judgment about those questions, that can be a pretty consequential role.

So I’d want to think about the marginal contribution in each place. Would joining a research organization let me do something that otherwise wouldn’t happen? Or am I more useful helping several organizations get the resources and people they need? I don’t think there’s a general answer that working directly on research is always better, or that allocating funding is always better. It depends a lot on the person and the opportunities.
